title: How to Unclog a Toilet

seo.title: How to Unclog a Toilet Without Making It Worse
seo.meta_description: If the bowl is rising, do not flush again. Learn the right plunging technique, when to use a toilet auger, and when the clog points to a larger drain problem.
seo.search_intent: Clear a clogged toilet safely, distinguish a local blockage from a main-drain problem, and prevent repeat clogs.

excerpt: If the water is rising, do not flush again. Let the level drop, use a flange-style toilet plunger with a good seal, and move to a toilet auger if plunging fails. If other drains are also slow or the clog keeps returning, call a plumber.
content_html:
A clogged toilet usually announces itself at the worst possible moment: you flush, the water rises instead of falling, and for a few seconds you are not sure whether it will stop. The first move is not to try again. Do not flush a second time while the bowl is high. If water is still entering or you are worried about an overflow, close the toilet's shutoff valve and let the level fall.

Most ordinary clogs affecting one toilet can be cleared with a flange-style toilet plunger and good technique. If that fails, the next sensible tool is a toilet auger. The diagnosis changes when other fixtures are also slow, gurgling or backing up: that can point to a blockage farther down the drain system rather than something trapped in the toilet itself.

Keep a clog from becoming an overflow first

If the bowl is nearly full, give it time. Many clogs still let water seep past slowly, so the level may drop on its own. While you wait, locate the small supply valve near the wall or floor behind the toilet. Turn it clockwise if you need to stop more water from entering the tank and bowl.

If you can clearly see an object that fell into the toilet and can reach it safely, put on gloves and remove it without pushing it deeper into the trap. Once a hard object has disappeared from view, improvised wire hooks are more likely to scratch porcelain or lodge the object farther in.

A plunger works because of the seal, not brute force

A flat sink plunger can sometimes move a clog, but a toilet plunger with a flange or extended rubber collar fits the bowl outlet much better. The rubber cup should be under water. If the bowl is unusually low, add enough water to cover the plunger rim.

Center it over the outlet and establish a tight seal. Make the first push relatively gentle so you expel water rather than blasting a pocket of air into the bowl. Then use firm push-pull strokes while keeping the seal intact. Ten to twenty controlled strokes are usually more useful than one dramatic shove.

If the bowl suddenly drains, remove the plunger and let it empty. Do not assume one successful drop means the passage is completely clear. Once the level is normal, add a modest amount of water or make one test flush. If the bowl rises again, repeat the plunging cycle before moving to another tool.

When plunging is not enough, use a toilet auger

A toilet auger, sometimes called a closet auger, is built to pass through the toilet trap while protecting the porcelain from the metal cable. That makes it a better choice here than a generic drain snake.

Seat the protective guide in the bowl outlet and advance the cable while turning the handle according to the tool instructions. When you meet resistance, work steadily rather than forcing it. You are trying to break through or retrieve the obstruction, not drive it farther into a pipe that is harder to reach.

Retract the cable, clean the tool and test the toilet again. If the auger will not pass, brings back evidence of a hard object, or the clog returns immediately, you have learned something important: this is probably not just a soft paper blockage.

What not to pour into a clogged toilet

A stubborn clog makes random chemical fixes tempting. Avoid turning the bowl into a chemistry experiment. Do not mix bleach, acids, drain openers, vinegar or other cleaners. Some combinations can release dangerous gases, and caustic liquid left in a blocked bowl creates a splash hazard for whoever eventually uses a plunger, auger or professional equipment.

Boiling water is also unnecessary. It does not replace the mechanical action that clears a toilet trap, and extreme heat is not something porcelain needs. If you already used a chemical product, do not plunge or auger blindly. Tell a plumber exactly what went into the bowl before they work on it.

A toilet that clogs repeatedly is a diagnosis problem

One clog after an unusually large amount of toilet paper may be exactly what it looks like. A toilet that needs a plunger every week is telling you more.

Look at what happens before the blockage. Are wipes, paper towels, hygiene products, floss or cat litter being flushed? Could a child have dropped a small object? Does the toilet have a weak flush even when it is not clogged? Do nearby drains gurgle when the toilet is used?

If several fixtures become slow or back up together, stop treating the toilet bowl as the whole problem. A main drain obstruction, venting issue or damaged pipe can require professional diagnosis. Continuing to send water into the system can turn a partial blockage into a sewage backup.

The best prevention rule is short

Toilets are designed for human waste and toilet paper. Wipes, paper towels, sanitary products, cotton swabs, dental floss and similar household waste belong in the trash. EPA guidance warns that materials such as wipes do not break down like toilet paper and can clog household plumbing, septic systems and wastewater equipment.

A small, lined trash can beside the toilet is a surprisingly effective plumbing tool if people in the household regularly use wipes or personal-care products.

When to stop troubleshooting and call a plumber

Call for help when correct plunging and a toilet auger do not clear the blockage, when you suspect a hard object, when the toilet clogs repeatedly, or when multiple drains in the home slow down or back up together. Sewage appearing outside the bowl is also a clear reason to stop using fixtures until the system is checked.

For a normal single-toilet clog, the useful sequence is straightforward: do not flush again, control the water level, plunge with a proper seal, and use a toilet auger if necessary. If the obstruction does not respond to those two tools or starts affecting other drains, it is probably no longer a problem you can solve from the bowl.

faq.question: What should I do if the toilet is about to overflow?
faq.answer: Do not flush again. Close the toilet shutoff valve if water is still entering, let the bowl level fall, and only then begin plunging.

faq.question: What kind of plunger works best on a toilet?
faq.answer: A toilet plunger with a flange or extended collar usually seals the bowl outlet better than a flat sink plunger.

faq.question: Should I use chemical drain cleaner in a clogged toilet?
faq.answer: It is not the first choice. Mechanical clearing with a plunger or toilet auger is usually more appropriate and avoids leaving caustic liquid in a bowl that must be worked on.

faq.question: When does a toilet clog suggest a main sewer-line problem?
faq.answer: If several drains become slow, gurgle or back up at the same time, the blockage may be farther down the drainage system and should be professionally assessed.
